doc.title: David Murray interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 18, 2003

title: His father, the church and civil rights leadership
summary: His father's activism through the church, the church as the strongest political force in the black community, and remarks on leaders and Martin Luther King.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: How did your father feel about your being involved in those kinds of things, even though it wasn’t a conscious choice, as you said, the circumstance kind of put you into it and you reacted.

Well my father is from the school of — civil rights was very high on his list. Even being a staunch church man, we believed in Martin Luther King, and that was the same year that Martin Luther King was killed. So my father was for anything that had anything to do with making the situation better. I mean the fact that he moved to Berkeley and put us in a better neighborhood than our cousins who lived in Oakland — I remember one of the most angry times that I’ve ever seen him was when my brother moved into a ghetto in Oakland. He went over there and made him move out because he said you don’t know how many sacrifices I had to make, being a garbageman and working extra jobs and doing this and that, for you to live in a city like Berkeley. So why in the hell would you go and live in a ghetto and put yourself at risk and now going to put my other brother at risk because he wants to live with you. I’ve never seen him so angry. So in his own way he was an activist. But not one that would join up with the Black Panthers or anything like that. But you know, just through the church you can express your anger. I think the church has been probably the strongest, I mean if you put it down for the year and years that they persevered, the church has been the strongest political animal in the black community, regardless of one speaker may raise up and be a communist or this or that, but the church has always been the overriding — it was always the place, even for them to hide if they needed sanctuary. The church would always take everybody back. And the church accepts everyone. The church, as far as acceptance, it’s ecumenical, churches. It takes everyone. Our church, The Church of God and Christ accepts everyone. There’s no lock in our churches. If a white man comes into our church we’re going to take him. If he’s down and out, come on in here and let’s get you together. And if you want to go on your way, fine. If you want to stay you’re welcome. That’s what church is. And to me that’s some activism right there, to me.
Because sometimes, you know after Martin and Malcolm, you get all these opportunist people and you know it just seems like that’s all there is you know. They don’t really
want to save the community, they want to be known for who they are. And they want to make themselves a leader. Most of the time a good leader just comes out of the people.
And they have their own agenda for themselves.

Yeah. I mean that’s a good leader. And that’s why Martin was so great because he just rose up through becoming a theologian to become who he was. I mean here’s a man who made his father change his name because he became a great man. He became Martin Luther. He wasn’t born Martin Luther, he was Melvin Lewis. And because he was a junior dad had to change his name too.
Yeah a lot of people don’t. But the people in Atlanta know that.
